q: Which fascial sheet separates the deep from the superficial perineal pouch?
x: The perineal membrane stretches between the ischiopubic rami. The deep pouch lies above it and the superficial pouch below it, down to Colles fascia.

w.Colles fascia: Colles fascia is the floor of the superficial pouch, the membranous layer of superficial fascia below the erectile roots.
w.Scarpa fascia: Scarpa fascia is the membranous layer of the abdominal wall that continues into Colles fascia. It never divides the pouches.
w.Obturator fascia: Obturator fascia covers obturator internus on the side wall and splits to form the pudendal canal. It is not the roof of the superficial pouch.
w.Buck fascia: Buck fascia wraps the erectile bodies of the penis, farther forward than the perineal pouches.

pt.say: The perineal membrane is the dark line between the deep pouch above and the superficial pouch below.

q: Which structure lies in the deep perineal pouch in men?
x: The deep pouch above the perineal membrane holds the external urethral sphincter, the membranous urethra and, in men, the bulbourethral (Cowper) glands.

w.Bulb of the penis: The bulb is the root of the corpus spongiosum, attached to the underside of the perineal membrane in the superficial pouch.
w.Bulbospongiosus: The bulbospongiosus wraps the bulb in the superficial pouch and squeezes out urine and semen.
w.Ischiocavernosus: The ischiocavernosus covers each crus in the superficial pouch and helps keep the penis erect.
w.Crura of the penis: The crura attach to the ischiopubic rami below the perineal membrane and continue as the corpora cavernosa.

pt.say: The bulbourethral glands sit beside the membranous urethra inside the deep pouch.

q: Where does urine spread after a spongy urethral rupture below the perineal membrane?
o: Scrotum, penis and lower abdominal wall
x: Urine fills the superficial pouch and follows Colles fascia, which continues into the dartos and Scarpa fascia, up into the scrotum, penis and lower abdominal wall. The attachments of Colles fascia to the rami and of Scarpa fascia to the fascia lata keep it out of the thighs and the anal triangle.

w.Retropubic space around the bladder: The retropubic space fills after a membranous urethral tear above the membrane, the pelvic fracture pattern, not after a straddle injury.
w.Medial thighs and buttocks: Colles fascia attaches to the ischiopubic rami, and Scarpa fascia fuses with the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament. Together they seal off the thighs.
w.Peritoneal cavity: Only an intraperitoneal bladder dome rupture spills urine into the peritoneal cavity. The urethra lies far below the peritoneum.
w.Ischioanal fossae: The ischioanal fossae lie in the anal triangle, behind the back edge of the perineal membrane where Colles fascia attaches. Urine cannot enter them.

hl: Spongy urethra torn below the membrane
pt.say: A spongy urethral tear fills the superficial pouch and Colles fascia steers urine into the scrotum, penis and abdominal wall.

q: Around which bony landmark does the pudendal nerve hook?
x: Leaving below the piriformis, the pudendal nerve crosses behind the sacrospinous ligament at the ischial spine before entering the pudendal canal, which makes the spine the pudendal block landmark.

w.Ischial tuberosity: The ischial tuberosity is the lower sitting bone. The pudendal nerve does not hook around it.
w.Pubic tubercle: The pubic tubercle is a landmark at the front of the pelvis. It is not related to the course of the pudendal nerve.
w.Anterior superior iliac spine: The anterior superior iliac spine is a landmark of the abdominal wall and inguinal ligament, far from the perineal nerves.
w.Sacral promontory: The sacral promontory marks the back of the pelvic inlet and the diagonal conjugate, not the course of the pudendal nerve.

pt.say: The pudendal nerve hooks around the ischial spine, the landmark used for a pudendal block.

q: Which nerve runs in Alcock canal on the wall of the ischioanal fossa?
x: Alcock canal is a split in the obturator fascia on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa that carries the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels forward to the perineum.

w.Obturator nerve: The obturator nerve runs higher on the side wall through the obturator canal to the thigh adductors.
w.Sciatic nerve: The sciatic nerve leaves below the piriformis and runs down the back of the thigh, never entering the perineum.
w.Inferior gluteal nerve: The inferior gluteal nerve leaves below the piriformis and turns into gluteus maximus, outside the perineum.
w.Ilioinguinal nerve: The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the mons and the anterior labia or scrotum. It does not run in the pudendal canal.

pt.say: The pudendal nerve runs in the pudendal (Alcock) canal on the wall of the ischioanal fossa.

q: Which branch of the pudendal nerve supplies the external anal sphincter?
x: The inferior rectal nerve leaves the pudendal nerve in the pudendal canal and crosses the ischioanal fossa. It supplies the external anal sphincter, the perianal skin and the canal below the pectinate line.

w.Perineal nerve: The perineal nerve supplies the urogenital triangle: the external urethral sphincter, perineal muscles and posterior scrotal or labial skin.
w.Dorsal nerve of the penis: The dorsal nerve of the penis is sensory to the glans and penile skin and supplies no sphincter.
w.Posterior scrotal nerve: Posterior scrotal nerves are cutaneous branches of the superficial perineal nerve and carry only skin sensation.
w.Pelvic splanchnic nerve: Pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic and act on smooth muscle. The external anal sphincter is skeletal and somatic.

pt.say: The inferior rectal branch supplies the external anal sphincter and perianal skin.

x: Pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2 to S4 are parasympathetic. They release nitric oxide that relaxes the helicine arteries and sinusoids so the corpora cavernosa fill: the point step.

w.Sympathetic, hypogastric: Hypogastric sympathetic fibers drive emission and close the internal sphincter, and sympathetic tone ends erection through vasoconstriction.
w.Somatic, pudendal: The pudendal nerve carries penile sensation and contracts the bulbospongiosus at ejaculation but does not dilate penile arteries.
w.Sympathetic, lumbar splanchnic: Lumbar splanchnic nerves carry sympathetic fibers from L1 and L2 for emission, not the vasodilation of erection.
w.Sympathetic, sacral splanchnic: Sacral splanchnic nerves come from the sacral sympathetic trunk and, despite the name, are sympathetic like the other splanchnics.

pt.say: Erection is parasympathetic through the pelvic splanchnic nerves: the point step.

q: Which node group drains the testis, unlike the scrotal skin around it?
x: The testis develops near the kidney and descends with its vessels, so its lymph climbs the spermatic cord to para-aortic nodes near the renal vessels. Scrotal skin drains to the groin instead.

w.Superficial inguinal nodes: Superficial inguinal nodes drain the scrotal skin, not the testis inside it. Enlarged groin nodes suggest scrotal invasion.
w.Deep inguinal nodes: Deep inguinal nodes drain the glans and the superficial inguinal group, not the testis.
w.External iliac nodes: External iliac nodes drain the bladder and the inguinal outflow, but testicular lymph bypasses the pelvis entirely.
w.Internal iliac nodes: Internal iliac nodes drain the prostate and rectum. Testicular lymphatics run above the pelvis with the testicular vessels.

pt.say: The testis drains to para-aortic nodes, where the gonadal arteries start.

q: Which node group drains the skin of the scrotum?
x: Scrotal skin is body wall that never moved, so like the vulva, lower vagina and penile shaft skin it drains to the superficial inguinal nodes below the inguinal ligament.

w.Para-aortic nodes: Para-aortic nodes receive the testis inside the scrotum, which carries its lymphatics up from its origin near the kidney.
w.Deep inguinal nodes: Deep inguinal nodes receive the glans and the outflow of the superficial group, a second station for scrotal skin.
w.Internal iliac nodes: Internal iliac nodes drain pelvic organs such as the prostate, cervix and upper anal canal, not perineal skin.
w.Sacral nodes: Sacral nodes in front of the sacrum receive the prostate, cervix and rectum, not the skin of the scrotum.

pt.say: Scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, below the inguinal ligament.

q: Which lesion of the anal canal typically causes painless bright red bleeding?
x: Internal hemorrhoids arise from the superior rectal plexus above the pectinate line, where visceral afferents sense only stretch, so they bleed bright red blood without pain.

w.External hemorrhoid: External hemorrhoids lie below the pectinate line under skin supplied by the inferior rectal nerve, so they hurt, especially when thrombosed.
w.Anal fissure: A fissure is a tear in the squamous lining below the line, usually posterior midline, causing sharp pain with each bowel movement.
w.Perianal abscess: A perianal abscess is an infected collection under somatically innervated skin, causing throbbing pain, swelling and fever rather than painless bleeding.
w.Anal squamous cell carcinoma: Squamous carcinoma arises below the line in somatically innervated lining and often causes pain, bleeding and a palpable mass.

pt.say: Internal hemorrhoids lie above the pectinate line, where visceral nerves make bleeding painless.

q: Where do the Bartholin gland ducts open?
x: The greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands lie in the superficial pouch behind the vestibular bulbs, and their ducts open into the vestibule at the posterolateral vaginal orifice, near 4 and 8 o'clock.

w.Beside the external urethral orifice: The paraurethral (Skene) glands, not Bartholin glands, open beside the external urethral orifice in the anterior vestibule.
w.Labia majora skin: The labia majora carry hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands. Bartholin ducts open medial to them, inside the vestibule.
w.Clitoral prepuce: The prepuce is the hood formed by the labia minora over the clitoris, anterior to the urethral orifice.
w.Posterior vaginal fornix: The posterior fornix is deep in the vagina behind the cervix, far above the vestibule where these ducts open.

pt.say: Bartholin glands sit in the superficial pouch, and their ducts open at the posterolateral vaginal orifice.

q: Which part of the male urethra is shortest and passes through the external sphincter?
x: The membranous urethra is the short part that runs through the deep perineal pouch, surrounded by the external urethral sphincter. Apart from the meatus it is the narrowest, least stretchy part, so pelvic fractures tear it.

w.Prostatic urethra: The prostatic urethra runs through the prostate and receives the ejaculatory ducts. It is the widest part of the male urethra.
w.Spongy urethra: The spongy urethra is the longest part, running in the corpus spongiosum from the bulb to the external meatus.
w.Bladder neck: The bladder neck is surrounded by the smooth muscle internal sphincter, not by the skeletal external urethral sphincter.
w.External urethral meatus: The external urethral meatus is the narrowest point of the whole urethra, but it lies at the tip of the glans, far from the external sphincter.

pt.say: The membranous urethra passes through the deep pouch inside the external urethral sphincter.
